speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Marchand (Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
maintopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege to announce the areas that, effective April 1, 1970, will be designated as "special areas", under the provisions of the Government Organization Act establishing my department. The areas are:
(A)	In eastern Canada, six urban areas where we expect that my department's incentives to industry will bring about substantially faster industrial growth. To support this growth, my department is ready to finance community facilities-water, sewers, roads, schools and so on-which are needed but
which the cities and provinces cannot afford. These urban areas of eastern Canada are as follows: In Newfoundland, St. John's and a surrounding area including the Conception Bay coast from Portugal Cove to Carbonear. In Nova Scotia, the metropolitan area of Hali-fax-Dartmouth. In New Brunswick, the city of Saint John as well as the city of Moncton and neighbouring areas. In Quebec, the city of Quebec and vicinity as well as the area of Trois-Rivieres, Shawinigan, Grand'Mere and Becancour.

(B)	In Saskatchewan the urban areas are Regina and Saskatoon.
These cities were not included in the designated region under the industrial incentives program of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, because they have in recent, years enjoyed very rapid growth. They are now, however, adversely affected by wheat and potash marketing problems. Under the departmental legislation, incentives will be offered to encourage alternative industrial employment.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
(C)	In Eastern Canada, three areas whose locations give them potential for growth but which may be held back by difficulties in financing community development. These areas are: in Newfoundland, Corner Brook and its environs; in Nova Scotia, the area round the Strait of Canso; and in Quebec, Sept Iles-Port Cartier.
(D)	In Newfoundland, six additional areas which contain resettlement centres for people moving from the outports. In some of these centres there is special need for improved water and sewer facilities for housing, schools and roads. The areas are: the part of the Burin Peninsula that includes Fortune, Grand Bank, Garnish, St. Lawrence, Burin and Marystown; the area of Grand Falls, Bot-wood, Lewisporte and Gander; the area of Stephenville and St. George's; the area of Hawke's Bay, Port Saunders and Port au Choix; the area of Come-By-Chance, Arnold's Cove and Goobies; the Happy Valley area in Labrador.
(E)	In the prairie provinces, three midnorthern areas that can be assisted by indus-

March 11. 1970
Designation of Special Areas trial incentives for the development of forest-based operations and other resource industries and which require improved community facilities, particularly to assist the economic and social progress of Indian and Metis people. These areas are: in Manitoba, an area around The Pas; in Saskatchewan, the Meadow Lake area extending north to Lac la Loche; in Alberta, an area centred on Lesser Slave Lake and including Whitecourt and High Prairie.

(F)	In Ontario and Quebec, two areas where improved employment and income prospects depend on encouragement to forest-based industry and other industrial incentives. These areas are:
Cl) In Quebec, the Lac St.-Jean area.
(2) In Ontario, the area including Renfrew, Pembroke, Arnprior, Bancroft and Barry's Bay.
The provinces concerned have been consulted about these designations, and the precise boundaries of the areas will be specified in agreements with the provinces.
The initial designations will be effective to June 30, 1972, the same date as for the present designations under the industrial incentives legislation.
The agreements that are now being made with the provinces will be for the same period as the designations. For most of the areas, however, it is expected that these agreements will be followed by further joint development plans extending over a five-year period.
The present agreements will provide mainly for priority projects whose construction can be started in the next few months. These projects will involve commitments of federal funds to an amount of more than $200 million.
That sum is, of course, for the financing of provincial and municipal projects, over and above our greatly increased commitments to the private sector, for industrial development incentives.
The first agreements will be signed shortly with Newfoundland and New Brunswick and will cover arrangements for financing highway construction as well as projects in the special areas.

speakeroldname: Mr. Walter C. Carter (St. John's West):
maintopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in the official opposition welcome the minister's announcement this afternoon. We have been waiting impatiently IMr. Marchand (Langeller).]
for the new department to come alive. The creation of the new department a year ago was heralded as a cure-all for the economic disparities in Canada, and this is the first indication that the minister or his department was even aware that these disparities existed.
We are happy, sir, that the minister has recognized that disparities exist in urban centres as well as the rural areas because some of the worst pockets of poverty in this country exist in the major urban areas.
The greatest curse in this country at this time is regional disparity. For the last 20 months the government has been giving lip service to its promise of a just society. Mr. Speaker, we feel that the great division in this country is not over language or culture but over economics-meat and potatoes. Eliminate the economic depression and there will be no threat to national unity in Canada. Confederation will take on more meaning, especially for the have-not areas, if what is outlined by the minister today is successful in erasing economic blight.
Some time ago in this House the Minister of Transport said that confederation has been a blessing for my province of Newfoundland. Sir, I agree it has been, but there are many promises which still have not been fulfilled. This program has been long awaited by my province, and indeed by all of the other have-not provinces.
We have not yet had the opportunity to study in detail what is planned, but this program is crucial for Newfoundland in order to get the province out of the financial mess in which it now finds itself. I think, Mr. Speaker, that eliminating the present scandalous unemployment in Quebec will once and for all silence those who preach separatism there.

maintopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION
speechtext:
The promised assistance for Saskatchewan cannot come too soon. People are moving out of that province at a rate greater than during the depression. I am told that approximately 7,000 people are leaving that province every year. I am also told that many car dealers there have been taken over by the automobile manufacturers because they just cannot keep going as private enterprises. In the Regina area alone a reported 1,000 homes are standing empty. The construction industry is in one of its slowest periods ever, and we are told that several farm machinery dealers are going belly up.
So far, Mr. Speaker, the minister's statement is merely words. If these words are
March 11, 1970

translated into real action I am sure members on this side of the House will be the first to give full credit to the minister.

maintopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to the extent that the minister's announcement will help areas of Canada facing economic problems, and to the extent that it will help people facing economic problems it will certainly be welcomed. But it should be remembered that the drawing of a boundary, or pointing at a specific community, is the last step of a process that will be meaningful only if it has been preceded by an adequate determination of objectives, what it is the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is setting out to accomplish, and followed by an adequate allocation of financial and other resources.
The government's announcement-I want to thank the minister for making a copy of it available to us, together with supporting material, earlier today-gives no information on the extent of assistance to particular communities, or the approach to be taken in providing assistance to the special areas established. Surely the government has had enough time since the department was established last year to develop a more adequate approach.
The confusion concerning the government's programs will be compounded as a result of questions which quite naturally will be asked concerning the reasons why primary, secondary and service industries can be assisted in the special areas just announced, and only secondary industry can qualify for assistance in the designated areas announced last summer. The programs of this department, if continued in this manner, will end up in one huge jumble. Unfortunately, ever since the new department was established its programs have been characterized by confusion, indecision and lack of adequate planning.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
In addition to the elimination of regional disparities the government has for some time attempted to delude the Canadian public with the impression that its regional development program is a major weapon in its war on poverty and is also a major weapon to counteract the adverse regional effects of its over-all economic policies. In both respects the government's policies have been a complete failure. Unemployment rates have continued to rise in Canada and are currently 6.1 per cent for the nation as a whole. It is admitted that unemployment will go higher
Designation of Special Areas before the winter is over. Such rates of unemployment for Canada mean unemployment rates of 10 to 12 per cent in some regions of Canada. The government's program has done nothing to reduce the disparity in unemployment rates and in over-all economic well-being.
It is also clear that the government's antiinflation policy is not working. It is succeeding in dragging the economy down in a way which increases unemployment without lessening the rate of price increases. The New Democratic Party for some time has called on the government to change the direction of its policy and outlined its own proposals in some detail in a minority report on interest rates and inflation last month.
When regional development legislation was before the House of Commons last summer, it was held up as the blueprint for future action and, in particular, the designated areas program under the Regional Development Incentives Act was regarded as the key.
The first major step announced by the minister last summer was the establishment of certain designated areas across Canada. Subsequent questions and inquiries have established that the government's approach on these areas was nothing more than a political exercise unsupported by any sort of satisfactory criteria. The government abandoned its growth centre approach talked about so much when the legislation was introduced.
Information obtained on the operation of the designated areas to date shows that in some cases government assistance amounts to 70 per cent of the total cost of the project. Canadians have a right to expect that the government should have some equity in the project when that proportion of public money is involved.
It has also been shown that a considerable portion of the grants offered are being given to foreign controlled industries. In fact, the government is encouraging non-resident controlled industries to take advantage of incentive grants as illustrated in the answer to a question asked by myself where it was reported that the department has advertised its programs in New York and Boston papers.

Mr. Speaker, I find it rather funny that the mi-

nister should announce the designation of 22 "special areas" in eight Canadian provinces.
At the last elections, in 1968, he said along with newspaper men that the least advanced regions of Quebec had voted for the Ralliement Creditiste. But I find that the "designated areas" in Quebec, precisely because they are underdeveloped, elected Liberal members at the last elections.
Mr. Speaker, two years ago, we initiated the establishment of designated areas in order to fight poverty effectively. And now, it is found that "special areas" are required because the designated areas have not solved anything. In a year or six months, the minister may perhaps designate extra-special, para-special or intra-special areas, to carry on the war against poverty.
Mr. Speaker, not only did the minister explain what was a "special area", but he also stated that the "special areas" had been designated by the federal government after consultation with the provincial government concerned.
So that is the paradox which we are now facing in my own district of Northwestern Quebec: Representations are made to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) for the maintenance of gold mining subsidies, because it seems that 2,000 gold miners are to be dismissed in the Val d'Or-Malartic-Rouyn area, as well as on the Ontario side.
The minister claims that we should discontinue subsidies to gold mines when we can certainly export our total gold production to the United States.
When designating 22 "special zones" a region which is directly affected is being omitted. Lake St. John region is considered to be a logging region. The minister knows that the North-Western Quebec logging region is equal to that of Lake St. John or any other in the province.
I would not like the minister to think I am against the Lake St. John region benefiting by special measures established but what I do say is that our North-Western Quebec region should likewise be designated as a "special region" and benefit from government measures because we are now facing a most serious situation economically, politically and socially.
I think the minister should look into the possibility of making it a special area and of preventing the closing of the mines.

The minister said that setting up an infrastructure would help those areas by the building of schools, roads, and so on. But there is an infrastructure not referred to by the minister, and it is the monetary infrastructure which keeps its diabolical grip over human beings and leaders alike, including the minister. The problem is not to be solved by the designation of such special areas, because neither the minister nor the government bothers to look for the trouble.
I know that the minister will make the headlines tomorrow in all media, especially on the CBC. I do understand that, but this is no solution.
Neither the CBC nor the press settles economic problems which have to be dealt with by a political philosophy resting on sturdy foundations. I therefore say to the minister that if the Social Credit system were implemented we would settle Canada's economic problems.

U.S. IMPORT RESTRICTIONS-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the terms of Standing Order 43 I ask the unanimous consent of the House to propose a motion based upon an urgent and pressing necessity which arises out of the following circumstances.
The President of the United States yesterday made a statement regarding restrictions on imports of Canadian oil by the United States. This statement, and a subsequent briefing by a United States official, leaves unanswered questions of concern to many Canadians, namely, whether the Canadian government will comply with the United States order inasmuch as, according to statements which have been made, the Canadian government is to be the agent in administering this cutback; whether the government intends to challenge any of the fallacious assumptions upon which this decision was based; whether it is the view of the Canadian government that the present level of exports was endangering Alberta's reserve capacity, whether the Canadian government was considering similar cutbacks if, as alleged in the United States briefing, the Americans had not decided to apply one, and whether the government does not consider that such cutbacks will destroy Canadian incentive for further exploration.
Questions
With leave, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton East:
That the subject matter of the President's statement on the marketing of oil in the United States be referred to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works, and that the committee report thereon not later than March 20.

[Editor's Note: The reply follows:]
1.	There is one section of the Air Regulations which deals with aircraft noise abatement. Section 516 (bb) of the Air Regulations states; "The pilot-in-command of an aircraft operated on or in the vicinity of an aerodrome shall conform with any directions made by the Minister relating to noise abatement".
Special procedures for noise abatement are published for the international airports at Winnipeg, Toronto Ottawa, and Montreal. While the same basic concept is employed at all of these airports, the specific procedures vary to suit local needs.
The three basic concepts upon which aircraft noise abatement procedures are predicated are: preferential runways for arriving and departing aircraft, departure-climb and arrival-descent procedures, and curfew.
An ideal preferential runway permits aircraft to operate to and from an airport with a minimum of restrictions while disturbing the last number of people. Departure procedures, which are most important when a preferential runway is not available, are tailored to suit local conditions. To provide optimum relief for noise sensitive areas adjacent to airports aircraft may, consistent with safety, be asked to: attain a certain altitude as soon as practicable after take-off, initiate a turn away from certain residential developments, climb at reduced power and rate of climb while overflying certain areas near the runway, or, operate without any restrictions whatsoever.
On the other hand, arrival procedures are less flexible: depending upon weather conditions, aircraft are to be aligned with the runway not less than 6 miles from the runway threshold, and maintain an altitude of 2000 feet above ground for as long as practicable before commencing final descent for landing.
Curfew is employed at two airports: Montreal and Toronto, between the hours of
Questions
midnight and 7:00 a.m. This restriction is applicable only to turbo-jet aircraft.
2.	Special studies related to aircraft noise have been carried out on behalf of the Department by National Research Council as far back as 1959 and 1960 at Montreal and Ottawa International Airports, and then again at Montreal in 1965. A study is currently underway at Toronto.
3.	The results of the Ottawa and Montreal studies were compiled as reports which served as a basis for aircraft noise abatement procedures in the early 1960's. The 1965 report on Montreal resulted in the installation of a central noise monitoring system for that airport, which in turn prompted a similar study for Toronto. An automatic monitoring system for Toronto is expected to be completed by summer this year.
At present, no new studies are planned. [English]

speechtext:
should like to say a few words on this legislation, Mr. Speaker, because I feel it is one of the most important pieces of legislation which has been brought forward this session. It has to do with car safety and it is not necessary for me to remind hon. members, or the general public, how important this subject is to every individual in Canada.
I take this opportunity to pay tribute to the Canada Safety Council for the important work it is doing in advising people of ways and means by which they may be able to overcome the difficulties which arise in connection with motor safety and thus avoid many of the accidents which occur on our highways. I should like to refer to two or three of their pamphlets. One of these, put out in connection with a car check campaign, is headed, "Periodic car checks". The theme is: check your car, and check accidents. This is very important. After all, if a driver looks after his vehicle properly and has confidence in it, the chances of an accident are tremendously reduced.
The council has issued another bulletin on the subject of driver responsibility. Responsibility, it points out, goes hand in hand with power-and this includes horsepower. In this bulletin the council reminds motorists that they are responsible both morally and legally for the safe mechanical condition of their vehicles. This leaflet, like the last to which I referred, speaks for itself. After all, responsibility must rest upon an owner or driver of a car to see that it is in fit condition to be driven.

A third bulletin put out by the Safety Council has to do with the diagnosis of defects in automobiles. It advises motorists to go to garages and service stations in which they have confidence and where there is likelihood that the work necessary to maintain vehicles in fit condition for highway travel will be carried out effectively. Motorists are told:
It is most important to see and be seen, so motorists should check their lighting systems, windshield wipers and mirrors to ensure that they are working correctly.
Reading these bulletins will acquaint motorists with many other ways in which they can take their cars on to the highway with a minimum chance of an accident. In connection with this bill I should also like to pay tribute to a former member of the House, Mr. Heward Grafftey, the former member for Brome-Missisquoi.

speechtext:
There were occasions when he was almost jeered in this House for his persistence in keeping this subject before the attention of the government. I think he deserves the thanks and the support of all Canadians for the tremendous job he did in calling attention to the importance of car safety.
Over the years we have heard much-as well we should-about the need for research into the cause and eventual cure of cancer and heart disease. These are generally recognized as the No.l killers of our day and age. Often overlooked, however, is the fact that the leading cause of death for persons in the age group 1-46 years is the traffic accident. I suggest that the money made available for research into the causes and prevention of traffic accidents is peanuts when compared with the amount made available for research into health problems. A greater effort must be made in the direction of auto safety because, unknown to most people, the lack of it has become one of the biggest social problems of our time.
Last Friday a debate took place in this House in connection with the social problems which have arisen because the centres of our cities are jammed with vast numbers of automobiles. Eventually, of course, it may be necessary to prevent private cars entering downtown areas and mass transit systems will be provided along modem lines to move people rapidly, at the same time eliminating a major cause of air pollution. But it would be
March 11, 1970



wrong to blame auto manufacturers and governments alone. I certainly do not believe that the auto of today is safe, but according to the Canadian Safety Council, 90 per cent of all accidents result from human failure. Of the 8 per cent attributable to mechanical failure, a goodly proportion results from the lack of proper maintenance.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
While the government has a great responsibility for highway safety research and education, a burden undoubtedly rests on the road user. The specifications for the national safety standards as set down in Hansard for January 29 include provisions for seat-belts. I agree wholeheartedly with putting teeth into the law as far as it concerns automobile manufacturers, importers and distributors. To sell a car without such equipment, or with inferior equipment, is criminal. If attempting to take one's life is still adjudged a criminal offence, I venture to suggest that to drive without a safety belt is an elaborate attempt at suicide and should also be viewed just as seriously. Indeed, I would go so far as to say that the non-use of seat-belts probably contributes as much to the death and injury of other persons as it does to the non-user. A seat-belt limits mobility, and limited mobility is one certain way of preventing motorists turning around to carry on a conversation with the back seat driver, or an irate parent turning to admonish the noisy children in the back seat.
The January, 1970, edition of Safety Canada, published by the Canadian Safety Council, reports:
An extensive safety belt survey conducted by the Alberta Safety Council from Sept. 27 to Oct. 18, 1969, disclosed that only 18.4 per cent of 43,057 drivers and passengers interviewed were wearing the restraining devices.
Volunteers interviewed drivers and passengers at service stations and car washes on four successive Saturdays in 29 towns and cities.
The survey was accompanied by a major publicity campaign involving the press, radio, TV, distribution of restaurant place-mats and the handing out of pamphlets to motorists by volunteers.
Of those interviewed, two-thirds had safety belts available, of whom 27 per cent of the drivers and 28 per cent of the passengers had them buckled up.
On the highways, 42 per cent of drivers and passengers with safety belts available were wearing them. But this figure dropped to only 19 per cent in urban areas.
The low urban use of safety belts flies in the face of facts showing that most traffic fatalities take place within a 25 mile radius of the victims' homes and at speeds of less than 40 mph.
We have talked in this debate and in the committee of introducing uniquely Canadian
Motor Vehicle Safety
standards and that we should not ape the standards of the United States. I could not agree more. The Canadian market is of such a size in terms of cars sold and dollars transacted that provision should be made for Canadian standards which would meet the conditions of our roads and our weather and the acceptance of our people. After all, we have highway and weather conditions in Canada that are not found in too many other places in the world.
We discussed in committee the necessity for a regular monthly check of mufflers as a result of the salt and sand that is used on our highways to melt the snow. For a starter I would suggest that one safety requirement for Canadian automobiles be that it would be impossible to start a car without first securing the seat-belt. I believe there has been some practical research into this idea, and while we may not like the taste of it, this sort of medicine is good for us.
The minister stated on January 29:
Here, if I may be permitted, I should like to pay tribute to the provincial ministers concerned who have shown at least as much interest in this matter as the federal government. They have also cooperated with us in every way-as the debate revealed and the subsequent questioning in committee-in order to ensure the maximum amount of co-operation between the two levels of government, because the federal effort alone would not be sufficient to make a significant improvement.
The federal-provincial discussions to which I have referred led to my meeting with the provincial ministers on September 4, 1969, when it was agreed that the federal government should assume responsibility for the safety standards for new motor vehicles manufactured in Canada and for motor vehicles imported into Canada. At this time it was also agreed that the provinces, under existing legislation, would undertake to ensure the safety of vehicles in use as well as the safety of replacement and additional parts for motor vehicles.
There apparently was unanimous agreement that at the federal level we could make the biggest impact on the problem by dealing with the new car manufacturer to ensure that as cars leave the factory they are in top condition. It was also agreed that we would work closely with the provinces to ensure, wherever necessary, that they would introduce the kind of legislation which would put their needs on all fours with ours in terms of replacement parts. I do not think this is acceptable. The provinces do not have existing regulations to complement this act and I see here no guarantee that they will enact legislation to protect the innocent purchaser of a car bearing the national safety

March 11, 1970
Motor Vehicle Safety
mark but which has passed hands once or several times since earning this seal of approval.
It was said the other day during the debate-and I agree with it-that this act should be broadened to the extent that it would cover the resale of cars in our provinces. There is sufficient federal legislation covering the movement of fish, grain and meat, and it would be common sense to include the auto in like legislation. Fish, grain and meat are movable, as is the auto. The big difference seems to be that while the first three items are consumed, the last named consumes.
I think provinces have generally lagged behind in setting standards for performance achievement and the maintenance of cars on their roads. However, I do feel that our own province of Ontario has set some fairly high standards in respect of the resale of cars and safety checks on highways. It would appear that the city of Vancouver, and I believe the city of Victoria, have their own motor vehicle testing stations. These cities should be commended. Such stations should be located all over the country.
As outlined in this bill, there will be heavy penalties for misuse of the national safety mark on motor vehicles. There should be equally heavy penalties for misrepresentation of this safety mark by those dealers who will use it as a selling aid for cars that should long ago have been conveyed to the scrap yard. I hope the government will take steps in respect of an education and information program related to the use of the national safety mark and national safety standards. Perhaps this could be undertaken by a branch of Information Canada.
In this connection, in respect of the participation of provinces there was an article in the news the other day which indicated that our percentage of accidents per capita was higher than in a great many countries of the world, particularly the United States. The article went on to indicate that one of the reasons might be the tremendous educational program they have had in the United States to teach young people how to properly control the horses under the hood. I feel our provincial governments are taking this matter into consideration.
As I said in my opening remarks, the motor car and driving the motor car has become such an essential and important part of every person's life that it ranks with almost any phase of our educational program in high

school, and it should be taught in high school. Proper driving methods and procedures should be taught along with academic subjects. In the city of Kitchener some years ago they adopted an extended program in their high schools. It is rather significant to note that a tremendous drop in car accidents in that community occurred as a result of this educational program.
The meaning of the national safety code should be spelled out very carefully to all road users. The limitations of the national standards should also be made very clear. At the same time, every effort must be made to intensify educational programs on proper road and automobile use. We must work to strengthen this bill by regular report on and examination of the regulations. One half of the individuals driving today have been or will be involved in injury-causing accidents this year in Canada, and we can expect some 5,000 deaths on our roads and nearly 200,000 injuries. These are the stakes. Let us hope that with the enactment of this legislation the stakes will favour the Canadian motorist.

Mr. Speaker, while I also do not wish to unduly delay the passage of this legislation, which in my view is very long overdue and really does not go far enough, I do wish to put something on the record in respect of the views of my party on this very important subject. There are some issues which cut across all party lines, and I think this is one.
Car safety and traffic safety in Canada involve the lives and well-being of all our people. It is surely a very important fact that for several years now 100 Canadians have been killed every seven days on our streets or highways as a result of traffic accidents. At the same time, some 3,000 others have been variously injured either in a minor fashion or so severely that many of them might as well have died. In addition to that, as a people we spend something in the order of $1 billion a year to protect ourselves from this traffic "unsafety" situation. This includes car insurance payments.
So far as the Canada motor vehicle safety standards bill goes, it at least is a start in the right direction. It's terms which will be incorporated through order in council, I believe, will follow exactly the provisions developed in the same area in the United States. These standards which we are taking from the United States were won over a period of
March 11, 1970

years from the heel-dragging motor vehicle industry in the United States. They are not altogether adequate for Canada. Indeed, they are not altogether adequate in the United States. They do not have within them, for example, provision for such Canadian requirements as what I would consider to be a Canadian rear-window defroster and a common bumper height standard. There are other areas such as tire safety. I do not think these things are properly spelled out in the United States legislation which we are now picking up. We also feel there is a lack of proper car safety standards in respect of exhaust pollution.
Before the transportation committee we proposed several amendments along the lines I have indicated which we felt were necessary. We were told, and I agree, that the legislation, particularly at the committee level, is largely a vehicle by which to incorporate the beginning of safety regulations. The regulations themselves will be fitted into the vehicle. We hope we will get more and more adequate regulations as time goes on. I must compliment the minister because he accepted in general terms one or two amendments put forward at the committee stage which I think are useful.
I should like to say just a word or two in order to underline one or two other aspects which in my opinion are related very closely to the motor vehicle traffic situation. One of these is car insurance. We feel that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs should work more closely with the Department of Transport in reviewing the present car insurance situation in Canada. On every dollar Canadians spend on car insurance they recover from car insurance premiums only about 65 cents or 70 cents. As I said, I think this is a matter in which the Department of Consumer Affairs and the Department of Transport could interest themselves.
Although the campaign for safer cars in recent years in North America has resulted in some reform in respect of some very dangerous ingredients, the auto makers seem to have designed their vehicles with a view to making an additional profit from the collision of these vehicles. Perhaps the car manufacturers took a cynical attitude in respect of the car safety enthusiasts when the car safety enthusiasts suggested there was a need for collapsible front ends for the protection of the riders. They have built collapsible front ends and rear ends. They have done this with a vengeance. They have added a bit of engineering
Motor Vehicle Safety
apparently to ensure that whatever the front end hits will also suffer the maximum possible damage. If another car happens to be hit, the repair bills from the collision will certainly spurt upward, as hon. members and many other citizens of the country can testify.
Bumpers which once performed a protective function for the vehicle are now eyecatching decorations with built-in lights, grilles, knobs, vertical and horizontal knives of assorted kinds and sizes, and sharp snouts, all guaranteed in the event of collision to do three things: first, send the car to the repair shop for expensive replacements; second, ensure that whatever is hit will be carved into appropriate designs thus forcing the owner to undertake costly repairs and, third, improve economics for the manufacturer of spare parts.
Testimony taken during the U.S. Senate subcommittee hearings on anti-trust and monopoly showed that from 1965 to mid-1969 new car prices for popular Ford and Chevrolet models rose by 10 per cent and for Plymouth models by 11 per cent. During the same period the price of replacement parts for Ford cars rose by 34.6 per cent, for Chevrolet cars by 19.9 per cent and for Plymouth cars by 22.5 per cent. Very briefly, this means that if a car which sells for $3,500 were rebuilt from spare parts, it would cost $15,000 for parts and labour.
Various tests have been conducted to illustrate the point I have been trying to make about the vulnerability of modern cars. This is not the time to go very deeply into this question. However, one test was made at five miles an hour, which is slower than the speed at which a Member of Parliament walks. The car was driven into a barrier. It resulted in damage in the amount of $200. The cars then backed into the same barrier at the same slow speed, and the damage averaged $214 in each case.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to conclude by urging the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) to follow the example of the Secretary of Transport in the United States in respect of sending out information. This U.S. minister is extremely active in this regard. I receive from his office no less than three separate releases each week dealing with what is being done by his department in matters which are important to life and death. I am not one to be easily enthused about things, but in my opinion the United States, finally, is really stepping up its safety program.

March 11, 1970
Motor Vehicle Sajety
I have received releases from the United States department concerning such things as tire standards, recall of faulty tires, inflammable materials used in the interior of cars, air pollution from exhaust systems, brake testing and recalls. They are particularly concerned about compliance with the requirements of car safety legislation. Public meetings are held by the department of transport at which consumers, dealers and others are encouraged to state their views on any matter of car safety.
Finally, as I say, there are three things involved in traffic safety-the car, the car driver and the road. This measure deals specifically with the vehicle. To the extent that this bill is on the road, we want to be sure it will continue in the right direction in respect of ensuring maximum traffic safety. [DOT] (4:10 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to participate in this debate, but since we are on the final stages of passage of the bill I thought I would put a few remarks on the record. I listened with some degree of interest to the last speaker, and I suggest to him that an old, gas washing machine motor and a tub with wheels on it would probably give him the kind of vehicle for which he is asking.
First of all, when we are dealing with this matter we must try to determine what the legislation will do to take care of existing problems in transportation in so far as automobiles are concerned, and discuss at some length some of the real hazards in the industry. The main hazards in automobiles are, first of all, horsepower and, second, speed. It seems to be a trend of the automobile manufacturers to go for bigger, faster and more powerful automobiles.
I suggest it is not at all difficult today to build a motor with an engine, a transmission and a differential that will perform as efficiently as the engines in today's automobiles, which will produce all the horsepower required under any circumstances and yet be limited to the road speeds that are permitted in Canada and the United States. I see very little sense in selling a Dodge Dart that will do 120 miles an hour to a 19 year old boy who is somewhat impressed with the appearance of the automobile but is certainly more impressed with its horsepower and the speed he can get out of the car. I say there is an inconsistency in our laws if we mark our highways, as is the case in Ontario, indicating

60-mile speed limit and then produce cars the main selling feature of which is the horsepower they can produce, when the speed which they can attain on our highways is in fact illegal.
A number of factors must be recognized when you analyse the general construction of an automobile, what it is composed of and what it is intended to do. When we speak about hazards and look at statistics, we find that a large number of the accidents that happen on our highways almost daily are caused by the failure of the operator to obey laws and signals or to recognize road conditions. But in many cases the accident is due to the failure of a component of the automobile. I suggest that this bill should impose on the manufacturers conditions that must be adhered to before the automobile can be put on the market.
One of the essentials of any automobile is a dual braking system. The braking system of automobiles should be manufactured to extremely rigid standards to assure the purchaser that, first of all, it will give the maximum braking effect and, second, that any wheel will operate independently of the others. Again, the national safety mark or the label that will be put on an automobile is really meaningless unless quality control is a rigid aspect of company policy. I think no government agency can guarantee the competence of an automobile within minutes of its leaving the dealer's showroom; therefore, quality control is essential.
The second important consideration which should be given by the government to the problems that we have on our highways is that money be spent on compulsory driving schools for any driver who was involved in an accident of any seriousness at all. Attendance at these schools must be compulsory.
Automatic dimming devices should be compulsory in all vehicles. I do not think it would be too difficult for manufacturers to consider a form of warning signal in the event of the failure of any component that could impede the safe operation of the vehicle. We should consider regulating a safety level for standard equipment such as automobiles tires. Not too long ago two-ply tires were standard equipment. Today there is a change in some areas, but two-ply tires are still available on the market. The standard should be the highest available grade of tire on the market, and the use of such tires should be compulsory. There is today on the market a first grade, second grade and third grade tire, and in most chain
March 11, 1970

or department stores there are unbranded tires or what we refer to sometimes as factory rejects. These tires usually sell at less than one-third of the price of first grade tires. The use of such tires should be absolutely prohibited.
I have the privilege of coming from the city of Edmonton where in the last year compulsory car check legislation was brought in. Every automobile in the province of Alberta within certain areas had to be passed at a car check centre. First of all, tests were made on the surface of the automobile only. The finding of the tests was certainly not conclusive and could not prove whether or not the automobile was roadworthy. The argument that so many people used was that the job was not done by experts and therefore was not successful. I received a number of letters from people who complained bitterly because they had been requested on the first examination to make certain repairs to their automobiles. Indeed, my wife when she took her car in was requested to do repairs worth $65 to her car, but having done the repairs the car was not reinspected: she simply went back and told them the job had been done, following which they handed her a car test sticker for a $1 fee. This is why some of these programs fail. I commend the minister of transport in the province of Alberta for having had the foresight to discontinue this program.
Again I go back to the old argument that we must recognize the problem where it begins. It begins when the car leaves the factory. If the car has not gone through a rigid inspection procedure, if quality control has not been one of the conditions of the automobile company, there is no way in which we will get a truly safe automobile on the market.
Most American and Canadian cars are constructed to give the ultimate purchaser the maximum comfort, the maximum performance, the maximum eye appeal and, I hope, maximum protection against all the elements. 1 think the government would do well to provide, if necessary, assistance to manufacturers to further their studies into every aspect of motor vehicle safety and to enlarge their quality control departments.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to see what is being done about auto safety through the provisions of this bill. I am sure it is long overdue and needs further additions. But I
Motor Vehicle Safety
would like to remind the House of one fact, which is that no matter how careful you are, accidents will happen. Recently I had a problem driving a car with two master brake cylinders on it. One cylinder apparently was low in oil, and the seal on the other one was broken. One morning, backing out of the garage I went to put on the brakes and found I did not have any brakes. As a result, the car and I went into a snowbank and I had to get a wrecker to pull it out. If this had happened on the highway there could have been a disastrous accident. I do not know how such things can be avoided. It seems to me it may be necessary to have periodic check-ups for motor cars. But this car had gone 25,000 miles and had been serviced regularly. However, since the brakes appeared to be working, apparently they were not checked. This is something that happened to myself within the last two weeks.

speechtext: If the hon. member would permit me, Mr. Speaker, may I say such a problem could be corrected simply by having hydraulic and mechanical brakes on the vehicle. That is the simple solution so far as the manufacturers are concerned.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for bringing up this point because I used to drive a Hudson, now gone from the field, and it had hydraulic and mechanical brakes. But because this other car had two master cylinders, apparently the manufacturers thought one set of brakes was sufficient.
I now wish to deal with the question of the massive air pollution in our cities and on our highways caused by the motor car. Those of us who have driven in a large city at rush hour, taking an hour or an hour and a half to get out of the city, have seen the carbon monoxide pouring out of the motor vehicles, rising up into the air and polluting the atmosphere of the city. Many people think we are moving too slowly to control air pollution. This is one of the criticisms that I hear frequently. We know that the motor car is one of the prime causes of air pollution, particularly in urban areas-an estimated 60 per cent. One university professor has gone so far as to say that governments are hiding pollution data describing the extent and the hazards of pollution. All of us who have been in places frequented by buses and motor cars realize the amount of poisonous gases that they give off.

March 11, 1970
Motor Vehicle Safety
Just a few days ago one well known Toronto medical man stated that 50 per cent of the diseases of mankind today can be traced directly or indirectly to air pollution. That is a frightening statement. And it must be considered in the context that fatal accidents, mainly automobile accidents-over 50,000 per year-are the greatest cause of death for those in the one year to 35 year age group. This shows that preventive medicine has pretty well halted the fatal effects of communicable diseases. Accidents have taken their place and, as I say, today they are the major cause of death for the one year to 35 year age group.
Hon. members are well aware of the number of motor car accidents which take place across Canada, over 150,000 per year. Today one bed out of every ten in our hospitals is taken up with an accident case, the majority of them being motor car accident cases. Leaving aside consideration of the suffering involved and the fatal tragedies that may occur, these accident cases are using up hospital beds that are sorely needed for medical and surgical cases. In addition there is the consideration that the federal and provincial governments are now paying for medicare. That means you and I. This is a pressing economic reason for doing something about the problem. That is not all, Mr. Speaker: I would remind you that many people who are involved in motor car accidents cannot return to work again-some are crippled for the rest of their lives; some are able to do only partial work. The economic loss is tremendous and far overshadows any cost of solving the problem.
Today I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) a question about air pollution at Toronto International Airport, and I wish to thank him for the answer he gave. I was pleased to hear he is doing something about it and that within a few years jet planes will not be polluting the atmosphere. But I would point out to the minister that at Toronto International Airport, in my opinion you encounter far more pollution when you go downstairs to collect your baggage and move out on the ramp where the diesel buses and motor cars come to collect travellers. About two weeks ago I was out on that ramp. It was pretty bad that night because some charter planes had come in, apparently all nearly at the same time. There was such a crowd around that one could hardly move. Traffic was congested. One car had stopped completely and people were waiting for a wreck-

ing truck to pull it away. You never saw such a jam in your life. People could hardly breathe standing on that semi closed-in ramp. The pollution caused there was far greater than that caused by the jet planes.
I could see people coughing and wiping their eyes. It reminded me of the occasion about ten years ago when I was in Los Angeles. One morning when I came out to go to the airport on my way home, my eyes started streaming. They were smarting and smarting. I wondered what was the cause. It was the air pollution: fog and mild rain held it at ground level.
This pollution problem must be tackled. Cardiovascular and respiratory diseases are the worst problems being faced by the medical profession today. They are presenting a real challenge to the medical profession. In many cases they are caused by air pollution, and the solution of this pollution must be tackled no matter what the cost. Too often we are prone to forget about the toll taken by car accidents when those accidents do not involve us personally. The cost of all this involves the pocketbook of everybody in Canada. We had better waken up and realize that the burden of looking after the consequences of air pollution and car accidents can become too great.

I expect the minister to look at the Toronto International Airport and others that present the same problems. I suggest to him that it should be possible to bring in some type of transportation other than diesel. Surely buses using diesel could easily be replaced, probably by buses which are battery-driven or use a low-pollution gasoline product.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks on Bill C-137 will be very brief because the bill has already been discussed in committee for three or four days; in fact, it has been so thoroughly discussed that there are approximately 250 pages of evidence. Most of the points have been raised and have been answered by the minister and his officials. I think everyone agrees that the principle of the bill is good, that everything that can possibly be done to make a vehicle safer should be done. I appreciate the minister's desire to have the bill passed in time to have some of these provisions effective in the current year.
I do not want to delay passage of the bill. However, there are one or two questions I would like the minister to answer in his final

remarks. No bill is perfect in its draft stage. There were a couple of serious flaws in the bill as originally drafted. After spending two or three days studying the bill, I felt I was barking up the wrong tree and there was something wrong with me, but eventually the minister and his officials recognized and corrected these defects. I am happy about this because there were serious flaws in the original draft of the bill.
The bill deals primarily with the importation of vehicles from the United States. The main criticism that we in the opposition had to the bill was that the penalties provided were not stiff enough. We discussed at length the fact that the standards were not laid down or specified in the bill. I can appreciate the reason for that. It might be better to pass the legislation first, then let the minister promulgate the safety standards. He supplied us with a list of 29 basic regulations.
I remind the minister of the commitment he made in committee. I asked him if, after the bill was passed, he would entertain representations from the committee or individual Members of Parliament as to new regulations that should be promulgated. The minister assured us that he would be very happy to listen to representations. He indicated that if he thought they were serious and worth while, he would implement them. I remind the minister of this commitment. I hope he will keep the commitment in mind when the time comes to redraft the bill and to make changes.
Some of the standards which we felt were not rigid enough have already been mentioned. One such standard concerns bumpers. Most people will agree the bumper on the present-day car is nothing but an ornament. It is a piece of chrome put on the car for appearance. It has no function with regard to safety. It is a piece of ornamentation. As the previous speaker mentioned, new types of bumper are being developed. I hope the minister and his department will consider the feasibility of these new types of bumper becoming standard equipment. There is also the matter of exhaust emission and pollution control. The minister indicated these would be taken into consideration.
I also suggest that the braking standards are not rigid enough. I was surprised to find that some of the higher powered cars, those with the most horsepower, have the lowest ratio of horsepower to braking area. This is ridiculous and should be checked into with

the manufacturers. Cars are being manufactured with higher horsepower, yet they are still using the conventional old-style brakes. This area should be studied very thoroughly by the department when the regulations are being promulgated.
I wish to make one more suggestion. I am still not happy about the provisions of compensation for seized vehicles. One of the things that bothered us in committee was that the original bill could conceivably give inspectors the power to seize a private vehicle. This was corrected when the amendment was made to clause 13. As the bill now stands, vehicles can be seized from the premises of a dealer. The only compensation the dealer can receive is under clause 14 (2), which states that the provisions of section 64 (a) of the Fisheries Act will apply to the new act. It seems there could be quite a lapse of time here. If vehicles are seized from a dealer under the provisions of the Fisheries Act, I understand there could be a lapse of up to 90 days. A vehicle could be held that long. The vehicle could then be seized, and the only provision under section 64 (a) of the Fisheries Act is that the owner is entitled to his equity in that vehicle. However, if the vehicle is sold by public sale and only realizes half its value, as I understand the act the owner would be entitled to only the proceeds of the sale. Possibly the minister could explain that later.
It can be said that this is a matter between the manufacturer and the dealer, that if the manufacturer values the dealer's franchise he will compensate the dealer for the loss of those vehicles. I feel there should be something in the bill to make the sanctions a little stronger against the manufacturer. If a dealer has in his showroom 12 vehicles that are seized and tied up for a period of 60 to 90 days, vehicles which have probably been financed under wholesale replacement, what does the dealer do for replacements in order to stay in business?
I hope the minister will answer these questions when he closes the debate. I support the early passage of the bill, although I still maintain it does not go far enough. I think it will give the minister a vehicle to bring into force effective regulations for vehicle safety.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to take up a great deal of the time of the House to recapitulate, as it were, many of the things I said in connection with this legislation both on second reading and in the committee. and most particularly to members of the Transport and Communications Committee, for their co-operation and for the thorough way in which they dealt with this bill. As was pointed out this afternoon by the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) and the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg)- or is it Moose Jaw-Skoberg?-we achieved in the committee advantages and benefits through the amendments I was very happy to accept. I think this was a good demonstration of how the committees system can work. I do not propose to go over all the points that have been raised this afternoon because, as I have said, it would take a great deal of time. I believe that the hon. members concerned have most of the answers, at least to the extent that I am able to give them.
With regard to the question of seizure raised by the hon. member for Moncton, he does know of the problems of limitation in that regard. Perhaps he might be satisfied if I indicated to him that I do recognize, as I do in respect of some of the other points he raised in the committee, that there is validity in what he said. This involves a matter, again, of the extent of our authority and competence. If experience shows we can do something to improve the situation, then we certainly will do so. I might say, too, that I think it is our intention to avoid to the maximum extent possible the likely seizure in the manner which he outlined and which would cause this problem.
In other words this act, when it becomes law, will be most effective if indeed we prevent cars which have discrepancies of one kind or another from reaching the point where they are in the hands of purchasers. It will only be in terms of a latent fault that this would result. I think we will be performing best if indeed the problem that the hon. member for Moncton outlined does not occur, because this will indicate that we have caught the deficiencies before they have reached that point.
Throughout this debate I think there have been one or two what I might describe as general inconsistencies. I do not say that in any critical sense. I think I ought to point this out for the record. One has to do with some of the matters raised by the hon. member for Moose Jaw about warranties and the obligation on the part of manufacturers to pay for such repairs or replacements as may be necessary. I do not believe it can be argued that these are matters falling within the ambit of this bill which is related to auto
Motor Vehicle Safety
safety. As I explained in committee, while I agree wholeheartedly that the user or purchaser of an automobile should not be penalized for something over which he has no control, I suggest to the hon. member and to the House that in fact this is a contractual relationship between the purchaser and the supplier which is only indirectly related to safety, and that therefore it does indeed come under provincial jurisdiction.
At least, this is the best advice we have been able to obtain, and it has been confirmed in a number of quarters. I mentioned that matter in particular because it leads me to the second point on which there has been major inconsistency in this debate. It has to do with those matters which are of federal jurisdiction entirely and those which fall within the responsibility of the provinces.
This legislation will not be as effective as I and all hon. members would want it to be unless we have the full co-operation of the provinces. I emphasize again that our jurisdiction and our authority extends only to new vehicles, only to the manufactured item as it comes from the plant. The instant it is sold, it becomes an object which for all practical purposes is under provincial jurisdiction.
Quite a few members, while pointing out very valid problems in terms of auto safety, I think failed to make a distinction and failed to recognize, to the extent that is necessary, the limitations upon federal power. Above all, the necessity for co-operation with the provinces is a recognition of this from the outset. This bill, when it becomes law, will not really do its job unless there is companion legislation in the provinces which is on all fours with the federal legislation. So there have been to date two separate federal-provincial conferences involving the ministers responsible in each of the ten provinces and myself. This has been an excellent example of federal-provincial co-operation.
There has been widespread agreement and recognition of the need for supplemental legislation by the provinces for such a thing, for example, as was touched on this afternoon-that is, tire safety and tire standards. It will not do very much good if the federal government says that tires on brand new vehicles have to be of such-and-such a standard, and the replacement tires purchased in provinces are not of the same standard. In this case the provinces will, I am sure, apply the same standards on replacement tires as we set up for new tires. I hope we can extend that principle to a wide range of replacement

March 11, 1970
Motor Vehicle Safety
parts so the provinces will be able to help us, and we them, in what is after all a common problem to all of us.
There has been some mention today of pollution. The hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard), who I know has a particular interest in the matter, was the primary person to mention it. When this bill was originally drafted, it was strictly an auto safety bill in the sense of protecting life and limb. We made a more exhaustive study of our regulatory powers and came to the conclusion that we could, in fact, regulate and define auto safety as having to do also with the preservation of health. It was for this reason I expanded the bill to include exhaust systems. As the House will know, I have indicated on earlier occasions that we propose to be as stringent as we possibly can in this regard. There is a good deal that can be done now, even, in terms of the devices that are to be employed.
As the House will know, in some states of the United States, and in fact in some provinces in Canada, regulations are either now in place or are proposed which will enhance greatly improved exhaust systems. This, I may say, is only a partial answer because some of the devices, while removing some of the noxious substances, actually create others which are at least as harmful and perhaps even more so because they are both invisible to and undetectable by the average person.
In our research and development section we must attempt, to the maximum extent that we can, to devise new forms of combustion fuels and, perhaps, better combustion engines. I have had considerable discussion wih my counterparts in the United States on this question, and I am pleased to say that our level of co-operation is very high. As the hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather) mentioned earlier, the United States government and the United States people are very much seized of this and they are moving ahead certainly as fast as we are, if not faster.
So we have at the moment what amounts to a tacit understanding, which I hope will eventually evolve into a formal agreement, that we will exchange information and work together, because whatever the merits may be of continentalism in other respects having to do with energy policies and the like, there is no question that the Canadian interest is obviously served best by continentalism in terms of aulo and highway safety and related matters.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
It might be interesting to this House if I were to say on a remotely related subject -that of air pollution from aircraft, to which the hon. member for Simcoe North referred today-that of course it is rather pointless for the Canadian government to move in this field unless there is companion action in the United States, because aircraft move back and forth across the border constantly. It is my considered view that in so far as the continent is concerned, we will make very significant improvements in this field in a relatively short time.
What will prove to be more difficult-and I am already attempting to do something in this area-will be to arrive at agreement internationally in respect of flights coming in from overseas across the Atlantic and the Pacific where there is not the same rapport, closeness or liaison as there is with the United States. Happily, it would seem that there is now this new awareness of the real danger of pollution. I hope we can extend this liaison to the international community as well.
These are just some of the matters which have been raised. I would differentiate between the problems in respect of automobiles which are wholly related to safety and those which are only indirectly related or not related to it at all. I do not say this in any critical sense, but I might point out that there was some at least superficial difference of opinion between the hon. member for Surrey and the hon. member for Moose Jaw.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw in effect said, "Let us go out on our own and create an all-Canadian car." I do not wish to overstate the case but I believe he was suggesting that we do the thing on our own. The implication is that in some way or another the great majority of United States cars are inferior. On the other hand, the hon. member for Surrey has been castigating us in his mild fashion for not going ahead as fast as the Americans. I suggest there is some inconsistency here; there are two points of view. However, I know that both gentlemen are on all fours in respect of their desire to get the best bill possible.
The question of bumpers is of continual annoyance, I expect, to all hon. members who think it is not they but rather their wives who become involved in small scrapes.

I have no problem in agreeing with the hon. member that something should be done about this problem.
From a research point of view we are learning about everything done by United States agencies. In fact, we are undertaking some studies on this ourselves. One can find many different types of argument on this question, even including the one which has a measure of validity-that in fact the collapsible or give-away bumper is an assist in highway safety. The fact that there is a breaking away means that the car is not so rigid that the parties inside will be hurt. This is only one of a score of new concepts. There are such things as the water bumper or the air bag for the interior of cars, which is designed to inflate inside upon impact so that the parties in a sense are surrounded by a cushion of air.
The hon. member who spoke at the beginning of the debate today referred to seat-belts and various harness arrangements. There is some disagreement on the efficacy of these in their present form. I do not think anyone would argue that they are not good when properly placed and when they are of the proper strength. Here again, our standards will enable us to test them constantly and to also ensure that as new developments come along in this field they can be implemented quickly.
I have one final comment. This is something I have tried to emphasize throughout. It is one Which, perhaps a little ironically in my judgment, throughout the debate and in the committee has not really obtained the amount of
Motor Vehicle Safety
consideration it deserves. I refer to the fact that an accident happens only because something goes wrong. In the opinion of all the authorities on the subject, including those within my highway safety branch, the No. 1 task is not to ensure that we have the safest of all vehicles, because no matter whether the driver has happened to have a drink or something, when an automobile accident occurs the No. 1 challenge in respect of highway safety today is to find out the cause of the accident, what causes it to happen.
This is where the real research is required. It is not simply a matter of the drunk or inebriated driver. There is the fact that 70 per cent of the accidents occur when a vehicle is travelling at a speed under 30 miles an hour, and the fact of the number of accidents which occur on straight pieces of highway at mid-day when there is only one person in the car. One must also consider the frame of mind of the driver who goes off the road under such circumstances.
While auto safety is unquestionably of enormous importance, the fact is that no matter how safe the car, we will continue to have a good deal of carnage on our highways unless we find an answer to the problem of the driver and the causes of accidents. Perhaps it is necessary to consider both the driver and the nature of our highways and ask ourselves whether the highways are being properly constructed. As the hon. member for Simcoe North mentioned, we have some of the finest highways in the world. Everybody says now we are out of the woods because, we have incredibly good roads, but this fact simply seems to amplify the number of accidents which occur. So the question is whether our highways are faultily designed in some way or another. These are some of the interesting challenges which we face.
Again I want to thank members for understanding the need for relative haste in getting the measure through the House. I hope it will start having its effect very soon. I hope we will hear from the automobile companies. I agree with the hon. member for Moose Jaw that their co-operation in this task is vital and that they have a responsibility to make known to the Canadian public what they are doing and what their intentions are with regard to compliance.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the minister I would be very pleased to inform the House again of the purpose of this amendment to the Cape Breton Development Corporation Act. I would like to begin by thanking the Standing Committee on Regional Development for the great dispatch with which it processed this bill through the committee and accepted it with some degree of unanimity and then reported it back to the House.
This bill is rather limited in its scope, although it is important. It does not change the structure of Devco, nor does it change its basic functions or basic purpose. It is intended to add to the financial powers of that corporation and to put it on a footing equivalent to that of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion with regard to special areas.
One financial capability was lacking in Devco's battery of financial tools. This was Devco's lack of power to guarantee loans which an industry might seek from the private sector in order to establish itself in Cape Breton Island where Devco operates. The corporation had already been granted the power to make loans, to give incentive grants and to take equity positions in industrial concerns which seek to locate in Cape Breton Island, in order to stimulate industrial development there and to diversify the economy of the island. But it did not have the power to guarantee loans which any corporation might secure from the private sector. That is an important financial instrument. Some industries are quite capable of making their own way without obtaining significant loans, grants or equity positions, but access to private capital markets would be facilitated for them if they had a guarantee of the repayment of the principal and interest from such a Crown corporation.
So the sole purpose of the bill is to give that power to the corporation, to give guarantees on the loans advanced by others to industries which wish to settle on the island. There is a limit to the guarantee that Devco might give. That limit is $100 million which covers both principal and interest. As I think hon. members know, Devco is authorized to make loans and grants and take equity positions up to the limit of $20 million. That $20
March 11, 1970

million ceiling is not affected by the proposed amendment. What this proposed legislation adds is a guarantee capability of $100 million. As I said, this puts Devco in the same position to exercise financial powers as the department itself in special areas, but it is the view of the department that it would be better if that power resided with Devco rather than be spread between Devco and the department. This would put the island in exactly the same position as other special areas so far as financial powers are concerned.
This is a straightforward amendment and an important one. It is designed to enhance the opportunities for the industrialization of Cape Breton Island. I will close my remarks by again thanking the committee for the expeditious way in which it brought this legislation back to the House.

speechtext:
The House resumed from Monday, February 23, consideration of the motion of Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale):
That the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization, in consultation with Mr. Speaker, be
4693
Broadcasting of House of Commons Debates
directed to study the question of radio and television broadcasting of the proceedings of the House and its Committees, including the legal, procedural and technical aspects thereof, and the question of arrangements made for reporters for the electronic media in the Parliament buildings.

maintopic: BROADCASTING OF DEBATES BY RADIO AND TELEVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising once again to conclude my speech in this debate I shall be as brief as possible in enunciating a number of reasons for my opposition to the introduction of television into the House of Commons. First of all, it has been said on more than one occasion that the same argument was advanced when Hansard was first proposed for a daily, written record of the debates in the House. It is now being said that the same arguments advanced against Hansard are now being advanced against the introduction of television into the House.
It seems to me that the two cases are not alike. Much goes on in the House that is not recorded in Hansard. Many conversations are carried on and a great deal of highly skilled lobbying goes on that is not recorded in Hansard. Many jokes and jests uttered in the House are not recorded in Hansard. Sometimes it must be difficult for the interpreters and the Hansard reporters, but it is a known fact that much goes on in the House that is not printed in Hansard.
If the proceedings in this House were televised, all this would be heard. A member rising to speak would either be speaking to an attentive audience or he would be speaking to empty chairs. This would not give a good impression to his constituents who might not know that the absent members-many of whom are to your right, Mr. Speaker-were at committee meetings or in a minister's office attempting to ferret out the reason for government interference in their constituencies.
Another reason against the introduction of television is that a member who may be making a good and logical speech might not know how to put it across. His delivery might be poor and he might be reading every word of his speech. This would appear on television, but it does not appear in Hansard.
9 (5:30 p.m.)
Years and years ago the rules of this House laid down that a member should not read his speech. That rule is still in effect. Why was it incorporated in our Standing Orders? It is because a Member of Parliament is sent here to represent the true feelings of his constitu-
