He is supposed to be able to speak from memory about these things and to tell how the application of a certain piece of legislation will affect his constituents, whether beneficially or otherwise.
A Member of Parliament is not supposed to pick up a speech written by somebody else, or even by himself, and read it. If television is introduced, each member will prepare his speech in advance. He will even have a tendency to act out the words of his speech. As I said previously when I had an opportunity to speak on this subject, a member will even pronounce words in a certain way to express the feeling that may exist in his riding about a piece of legislation, not because he feels that way about it but because he thinks his constituents believe he should feel that way.
If there is one thing I detest today, it is the widespread feeling about the phonyness of politicians. Too many people across Canada say, "He is just a politician. Does he really mean what he says, or is he acting out a part"? I know some hon. members could not be actors even if they tried, but others would sure love to try-and television in the House would encourage them. It would be detrimental to the logic of the arguments they present in this House on behalf of their constituents. For that reason alone, Hansard and television are two different things.
I have mentioned that television would show the number of empty seats in the chamber. If this afternoon's proceedings were televised, showing all the empty seats to your right, Mr. Speaker, people in western Canada would naturally assume that since there is no western minister in the House the government is not concerned with their problems. They would make a snap decision on the basis of television. I should also point out that once introduced in this chamber, the televising of our proceedings would likely continue forever. In my opinion, Members of Parliament should make their arguments coolly, logically, and in a rational manner, in accordance with their beliefs in the kind of Canada that they want.
Some mention has been made that television could be extended to the proceedings of our committees. Although it may surprise some hon. members who have listened to me on this subject, I believe that would make more sense. If I have time this afternoon, I


may deal with the question of television in our committees.
What would television in the House of Commons really mean?
It would mean televising its proceedings in their entirety from two o'clock in the afternoon until ten o'clock in the evening, and this would require practically a whole new network across Canada. What about the enormous cost of that? Has anybody thought about that? I know the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) has had a great deal of experience in the television field. Can you envisage the enormous cost of establishing a whole new network to hear politicians expound on the glories of their constituencies and on how they think legislation will affect their constituencies?
At the close of the last session of Parliament, last July, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said, "We have to get these bums out of here. They are using the House of Commons as a soap-box to spread their ideas all across Canada." Mr. Speaker, if we had television in the House of Commons the bums might want to hang around a lot longer, at least some of those who profess to be good actors on television, and the Prime Minister would have much more difficulty getting legislation passed.
But let us examine the matter a little further. Who is going to watch the televised proceedings? Who has time? In my opinion, only those who have retired, who are over 65 years of age, and instead of watching a movie on a particular they may want to watch the House of Commons for an hour or two. But anybody engaged in earning a living does not have time to sit down and watch the House of Commons on television. On occasion someone who is ill at home, or a man who is babysitting while his wife is at the dentist, may turn on the television set for a half hour or so. Such casual viewers do not understand the working of Parliament. They do not know why those seats opposite are empty, why somebody down in the corner is talking to a friend instead of listening to me, and why somebody else is walking out of the House. As a result, they will make incorrect interpretations of the situation.
The cost of a completely new television network would be practically prohibitive for any sane government. There is some question of whether the present government is sane or not, but let us give its members the benefit of the doubt.

Let us say they are sane. If so, they will see the prohibitive cost involved. But there are those who advance, as an alternative, the televising of our proceedings for a two-hour period, covering motions, orders of the day and part or all of the question period. What would happen in the case of motions, Mr. Speaker? In recent years we have had five political parties represented in this House. Now there are four. On motions a minister gets up and makes a statement. I am one who has complained that ministers do not make enough statements on motions, that they make too many outside the House on television. But if television is introduced here, will that prompt them to make more statements on motions? For example, let us say a minister has a statement to make on the reorganization of his department and he makes it in the House of Commons. He will take up a certain amount of time. We had that experience today with a statement by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Mar-chand). His statement was commented upon by one member from each of the other parties.
As I say, we have only four parties now. In years to come we may have five again, or even six, as somebody suggests. In that case five statements, all in critical vein, will be made in reply to a minister's statement. In these circumstances a minister would be reluctant to make a statement on motions in the House, whether on the reorganization of his department or the establishment of departmental offices across Canada, as was the case today. Because he would have to face five critics he would be tempted to go down the hall to the television room and have his statement telecast from there, where there is no one to criticize him unless the television interviewer wishes to call in one or two critics.
Let us not be fooled by the argument that a televised two-hour period would enhance this House. Let us project this thing a little further. Let us suppose we have disposed of motions and have moved into the question period. Normally the question period is 40 minutes. Today it was mainly taken up with questions posed by members of the opposition, but from my study of the rules I do not see that the question period is reserved exclusively for opposition members. From time to time government backbenchers have expressed dissatisfaction at the decisions 21774-201

[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
It is a simple case of arithmetic. There are 264 members in the House excluding the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker. The government is in power, so it will more than likely have the majority of seats or it would not be in power. Even taking out the cabinet ministers, they will more than likely still have just as many members in their backbenches; and if you include the Parliamentary Secretaries you will probably have more than the whole combined opposition.
It is logical to assume that in a close and hard debate over the question of the allotment of the 40 minutes televising of the question period, government backbenchers would demand 20 of the 40 minutes, which would leave the official opposition with 20 minutes. The parties to my left would not be particularly happy with that. They are noted for being quiet, but from time to time they may want to raise a few questions. They could argue that their party should be allowed five minutes. So lest we think the question period would be enhanced, the official opposition would be allotted ten minutes, the NDP would be allotted five, the Ralliement Credi-tiste would be allotted five and the backbenchers of the government would be allotted 20.

The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cote) asks, "How about the answers?" That is what I was coming to. Let us suppose the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) asked a particularly embarrassing question of a particularly capable or verbose minister such as the Minister of Transport. He is very capable with words, but how capable with action we have yet to judge. But suppose he was asked the question-does anybody in this House think he could not talk for ten minutes? We would be surprised if he could not, because we know he is great with words and that there are a number of cabinet ministers who are perhaps just as good. We would have lost the ten minutes allotted to the official opposition for that day. From time to time we have heard backbenchers complain that the Speaker does not recognize
4696	COMMONS
Broadcasting of House of Commons Debates them as often as he does the front row. They can rest assured that if television comes in during the question period, they will not even be bobbing up for a question. The same principle applies to the two parties to my left.
Let us look at the 20 minutes that will be absorbed by the backbenchers of the government. Say, for example, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Douglas) wants to ask a question of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) which concerns his riding. He does not want to fall out with the minister because he may want to ask a petty favour in the future, so he sends notice of the question to the minister. The department tells him how to word the question so that the minister can answer it politely and look good. It is all a great show. Over a period of ten years of steady watching, I suppose the Canadian public would catch on that the whole dang thing is just a sham, that it is just a great show, and would realize that it was a planted question. It would be obvious that the whole 20 minutes was purely for show.
The whole purpose of the question period is to solicit information on the intentions of the government in running this country, not necessarily to give notice but to try to pierce the armour to see if there is any weakness in their administration or their intention in the application of a particular piece of legislation. In my opinion, with television in the House of Commons the question period would eventually be destroyed.
Let us go a step further and study the role of the House of Commons. Many people complain that it is a dead place, that nothing happens here and that everything takes place in committees. Yesterday was a good example. There were eight committees sitting, so 'the House was rather empty. I was in the agricultural committee in the morning and then in the transportation committee until ten o'clock at night. We had a pretty good attendance there. We had the Minister of Communications (Mr. Kierans) right on the firing line and things were pretty hot at times. With eight committees sitting at the same time, television would not bring members back into the House if they had a duty in the committee. Just because the transportation committee was not televised and the House was, I would not like to think that I had deserted the cause of my constituency and left the committee because I had no chance of getting on television there. Surely a Member of Parliament is not sent here just to sit; he is sent

DEBATES	March 11, 1970
here to work, to use his energy. As long as there are eight committees sitting during the day, whether or not this House is being televised surely duty will come before show in the eyes of many representatives on both sides of the House.
What will be the role of television commentators? Let us suppose that the two hour period, or the whole of the proceedings of the House of Commons is televised. Few people have a chance to watch it regularly-perhaps just those who happen to be ill or are retired. I suppose we still watch television to some extent at home in the evenings, watching the eleven o'clock news and the weekly commentaries and educational shows, etc. Who is going to do those weekly commentaries?
We have just had a debate in this House which hinged on pollution to some extent. Let us suppose that for some reason or another the debate came up in a hurry and the member handling it was not able to bring all his facts with him and consequently was not able to do the job of which he was capable. He does not have 17 research assistants, as have some of the big T.V. commentators. These people can prepare themselves very well for a 15, 20 or 30-minute show on the weekend. They can roll back reels of film of the time when the question was debated in the House and say, "Didn't that Member of Parliament, when he was speaking on pollution, know that 77 per cent of the air pollution in major cities is caused by the automobile?" I just throw that figure out as an example. If television is brought into the House of Commons, the T.V. commentators will assume the role of the opposition to the government more so than they do today.
It is no wonder that the great Pierre Burton and Charles Templeton-the first two that come to my mind-say they are all for it, and that in this technological age it is ridiculous that television should not be in the House of Commons. They think it should, Mr. Speaker, but it should enhance them so that rather than pick holes in my arguments, they can pick holes in me and my ability to push ideas across. It is not that they have ever done it, or that I have any particular grudge against those two commentators. However, it would only enhance them, and not the members who participate earnestly and to the best of their ability in the debate.
Now let us take a quick look at the role of a representative. A Member of Parliament is sent here to concern himself with the prob-
March 11, 1970
lems of the country and his constituency. Those problems take him all the way from the acreage payments announced a week ago by the minister to the Indian Affairs problem, to the oil problem, to the depths of foreign affairs and to the depths of our military role in the western alliance.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Some of the problems are big; some of them are little. It may seem surprising that it is the little things that concern the people back home. They may be personal problems about which a member has to see a minister, deputy minister or someone in the department. The member must say to that person, "Why wasn't so-and-so given a passport? Why is it being held up? Why wasn't such-and-such a corporation given a grant by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion? A member must be capable of making arrangements to see ministers and deputy ministers. He must be determined enough to pursue the little problems through the bureaucratic empire in Ottawa.
A Member of Parliament should not have to be a television actor capable of presenting arguments before the television cameras every day. I wish to deal with a Member of Parliament who may be very congenial and good at getting in to see ministers or their assistants about the little problems of his constituents, but cannot make a good speech off the cuff. Maybe he cannot talk about any given subject. If television comes into the House of Commons, every constituent in Canada will be watching to see if his member speaks.
If they do not see their member on television making a speech in the House of Commons, they will say, "So-and-so is up all the time, but I haven't seen our member. Where is he? Why isn't he here? Whether he likes it or not, the member will be judged by the number of times he participates in a debate that is being televised. What he says will not be important; what will be important is how he participates in the debate. They will be looking to see whether his hair is combed, what is the colour of his suit, the colour of his eyes, or how well his tie matches his shirt. That is not the reason a member is chosen to represent his constituency. He is not elected solely on his ability to expound at great length on any given subject without having been given notice. He is chosen because of his concern for the people in his riding, his desire
Broadcasting of House of Commons Debates to work for them and try to better then-position in life. Television in the House of Commons would not enhance this aspect of Parliament at all. We have a very serious matter here with which Members of Parliament must concern themselves.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments on the motion under consideration, which reads as follows;
That the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization, in consultation with Mr. Speaker, be directed to study the question of radio and television broadcasting of the proceedings of the House and its Committees, including the legal, procedural, and technical aspects thereof, and the question of arrangements made for reporters for the electronic media in the Parliament Buildings.
Mr. Speaker, this is a very important piece of legislation because it will be possible, through the media, to reach the people and to acquaint them with what is going on in the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, one can but commend the idea of informing the public, but I wonder if the best way of reaching the public was considered in the proposed measure.
I listened attentively to the comments from the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner), and I subscribe to several of his observations. For instance, he expressed concern about the course that could be given to the question period, as government back-benchers could prepare in advance their questions for the ministers so as to enable them to indicate the government policy. And if the Liberal backbenchers had the least bit of imagination, they could do exactly the same thing now. There is nothing to prevent a government member to put whatever questions he wants. In any event, they have done so on several occasions.
This can therefore not be argued against televising the debates of the House. It should be realized that the viewers do not have the advantage or privilege that we enjoy, since we are paid to be here, of following every day the debates of the House in front of their T.V. set.

speechtext:
The Honourable John Munro and The Honourable James Richardson announced today that the federal government has agreed to pay to the city of Winnipeg an additional grant of $589,516.00 to cover the city's share of the deficit of the 1967 Pan-American games.
Mr. Richardson stated that a letter was being delivered today to Mayor Stephen Juba informing him of the government's decision.
With the approval of this additional grant, the federal government has paid a total of $2,839,516.00 or 46 per cent of the total cost of holding the Pan-American games in Winnipeg. This includes the $750,000 federal grant, or 50 per cent share of the cost of the Olympic Pan-American swimming pool which is now in active and continuous use in the city.
In the final accounting, the federal government has paid 46 per cent of the total cost of the games, the Government of Manitoba 42 per cent and the City of Winnipeg 12 per cent.
March 9th, 1970
His Worship Mayor Stephen Juba,
City of Winnipeg,
Manitoba, Canada.
Dear Mr. Mayor:
I am very pleased to inform you that the federal cabinet has agreed to cover your administration's deficit with respect to the 1967 Pan-American games by making a grant to the city of $589,516.00.
I know you will share my great personal satisfaction that this very pressing problem for Winnipeg has been resolved. As you know, Canadians from coast to coast took justifiable pride in the outstanding success of the Pan-American games and the federal government's decision to make an additional financial contribution is a reflection of the widespread appreciation for the contribution made by Winnipeg to Canada's centennial year.
For Winnipeg, the Pan-Am games represented a prodigious community achievement in which thousands of Winnipegers contributed time and effort. The financial support received from all Manitobans and from all Canadians was, of course, vital, but the work, the enthusiasm, the drive and the imagination were of the authentic Winnipeg variety. I am delighted that our city's great contribution to centennial year is receiving this further recognition from the government of Canada.
Sincerely,
James Richardson.
Thursday, March 12, 1970
